<reason>PRO framed the motion around the worker whose security is actually in doubt and held that frame under real pressure. CON's best material—"zero is the wrong counterfactual," debt offset, leakage, the default-as-ceiling—genuinely shrank PRO's gain, but never showed that a larger deduction produces any balance for the non-participant. Under pressure question Q1, CON conceded "no deduction nudges him directly" and tried to relocate the debate to workers without plans, which quietly swaps out PRO's warehouse worker (who had an unopened packet) and then runs into PRO's escalation point: for everyone with a plan, defaults move the stuck middle at zero Treasury cost while a deduction still requires the decision the worker isn't making. CON's closing also misdescribed PRO's match argument as a surrender when PRO's point was that the auto-enrolled worker captures a match the non-participant forfeits in both worlds. CON's concession-stacking and "remainder vs increment" weighing was well constructed and keeps this competitive, and PRO's clipped rebuttal is a small execution cost, but PRO made the decisive question—who is actually moved—clearer and answered it.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's A2.1/A2.2 ("every hazard CON describes is a hazard of having money; his alternative avoids them by ensuring the worker never has any"), reinforced by A4.2's "fraction of something vs all of nothing," forced CON in B4.1 to admit deductions don't reach the non-participant—an admission PRO's closing turned into the deciding weighing.</best_rebuttal>
